title: Krishna's embassy to the court
hookLine: Krishna speaks for peace before the whole Kuru court, Duryodhana walks out, and a plan to seize the envoy ends in a laugh
carry: dharma tries peace first, even expecting a no
tomorrow: what does Krishna tell Karna on the road?

lines: A CHANCE TO STOP THE WAR.
cards: Morning in the great hall of the Kurus. Every seat is filled: Dhritarashtra on his throne, Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Duryodhana and his brothers, Karna beside them. Krishna walks in, and the hall goes quiet.
This is the moment the whole Udyoga has been building toward: a formal chance to stop the war, spoken face to face, in front of everyone who matters.

teach.b: Krishna speaks to Dhritarashtra first, and his argument is simple. You can stop this. Your sons and your nephews could stand together, and no one could stand against them.
Peace would be your gain, not your loss. Give the Pandavas their share. Others speak after him.
Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to make peace. Duryodhana hears them, and refuses.

teach.h: NOT EVEN A NEEDLE'S POINT OF LAND
teach.b: He says, in effect, that he won't give the Pandavas even as much land as the point of a needle would cover, and he walks out of the hall. Then Gandhari, his mother, is sent for.
He is called back to hear her, and she tells her son plainly that a person who can't rule his own anger and greed can't rule a kingdom. He leaves again.

teach.h: A PLOT, A LAUGH, A BLAZING FORM
teach.b: Outside, he and his friends make a plan: seize Krishna, tie him up, and the Pandavas will be helpless. Word reaches the hall. And Krishna laughs.
The text says that as he laughed, his body blazed, and gods and heroes seemed to stream out of him, so bright the court had to shut their eyes.
Only a few could look: Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the sages, and Dhritarashtra, granted sight for that moment. Then the vision ends, and Krishna walks calmly out. Think about that.
The one who could blaze like that came as a messenger, and asked. The night before, at Vidura's, he said he had come so no one could blame him for not trying.
Many Hindu teachers point to this embassy when they say dharma tries peace first: a war fought by dharma comes only after peace has truly been offered.
Krishna made the whole case in public, where no one could say it was never offered.

how: Krishna's embassy to the Kuru court is retold in Hindu storytelling and performance, and the form he reveals in the assembly is heard by some readers as a glimpse of the vision later shown to Arjuna.

o: the blazing form Krishna shows the Kuru court
the needle's point of land Duryodhana refuses
the getting ready, where peace is offered at court

games.q: the Kuru assembly — tap the pairs.
p: not a needle's point of land

s: Bhishma and Drona urged Duryodhana to go to war
they urged him to make peace, as Krishna did.
Gandhari counseled her son in the assembly
she told him that someone who can't rule his anger and greed can't rule a kingdom.
Krishna came to the court only because he expected Duryodhana to agree
he said he came so no one could blame him for not trying: dharma tries peace first.

games.q: you're at the Kuru court. Krishna could end this with the blaze everyone just saw. why does he come as a messenger and ask?
o: he wants to lure them into a trap.
dharma tries peace first; it has to be truly offered.
he isn't sure who would win a war.
games.why: he said he came so no one could blame him for not trying. even the one who blazed like that made the case for peace first.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're at odds with. Many Hindus close a prayer with Om shanti, shanti, shanti: peace, three times. Breathing slowly, say it for them.
If you don't pray, simply wish them peace, and think of one fair thing you could still offer, even if you expect a no.

wordCard.voice: Udyoga. The getting ready, where Krishna makes the case for peace in front of the whole Kuru court, and Duryodhana refuses.

orig.note: effort, getting ready; the embassy in the assembly is a public effort for peace.
